artboards.title: Home — the job as ground, not a lane
A — Logging a verdict, in place
B — The year with the job on it (chosen)
D — The wall you walk through
E — The why, and what it used to say
F — What happens after you log

annotations.text:
THE TEST FOR WHETHER SOMETHING IS A LANE: could it go quiet for six weeks without you noticing?

If yes, it is a lane — the silence is the finding, and the rail is how you see it.
If no, it is not. The job cannot silently go quiet; you would be unemployed. Drawing fifty-two identical fat bars for it is decoration, not information.

And on overlap: one lane per block, and the choosing IS the reflective act. But that only survives contact with real life if the moment of hesitation is rare. A good lane set is one where roughly nine blocks in ten are obvious and the tenth makes you think for two seconds. If every block is ambiguous, the lanes are wrong — not the rule.

Four lanes here, down from six. MONEY is gone: Cadence already does it, and a lane that duplicates a tool you already use produces no surprise. THE JOB is gone as a lane — see the variant below. What remains are the four that can go quiet on you.

Four rails, 81px each. Fewer lanes means bigger marks, more air, and a year view you can actually read.

WHY 'THE WORK' HAD TO GO. It was the right idea with a name that swallows everything: the portfolio is the work, the steps are the work, the body is the work. Every lane except the job is 'the work' — it is the name of the app, not of a lane.

So name lanes by their OBJECT, not their spirit. CRAFT is being good at something. RECOVERY is meetings, the 12x12, the step writing, the call you made instead. Both are the summons; only one is about becoming good at a thing.

RECOVERY rather than SOBER, because SOBER names a state and the lane holds hours. If sobriety itself wants recording, it is the same shape as the job: a condition, not a stack of blocks. PROGRAM would work too, and is what you would actually say out loud.

All four names are placeholders. Change any of them in one line.

The job as ground rather than as a lane.

One verdict a day — did it enlarge or diminish you — with no size, because the size is always the same and you already know it. Blank on a day off, which is why the ribbon has gaps exactly at weekends without anything drawing them.

The volume of the job carries nothing. The valence carries a great deal: 'it took the same forty hours every week and stopped enlarging me in March' is a finding, and it is invisible in every other tool you own.

LOCKED. B FULL / FADED for the day mark, 1 STACKED for the week cell.

One rule holds at both resolutions: footprint means size, fill means enlarged, fade means diminished. Rejected options kept and dimmed — a decision without its reasons is just a preference.

A — HOW YOU LOG A VERDICT.

No screen and no prompt: the ribbon cell IS the control. Tap today's cell and three cells open in place under the row; tap one and it closes. Two taps, no navigation, and the day grid never leaves the screen.

This is deliberately not the 3x2 grid. There is no size to pick, so a full screen for one bit of information would read as a chore — which is exactly how a daily ask turns into a streak you resent.

NO WORK is the third cell rather than a default, because a day off is a real answer and the app should never guess it from the calendar.

Skip a day and the cell stays blank. Nothing counts it, nothing mentions it, and no badge appears.

B — THE YEAR, DECIDED.

The job is drawn the way a lane is drawn: one bar a week, the same length every time, with only the solid/faded split moving. One encoding rule, not two.

The day-grain version — five 4px marks a week — was drawn beside this one and dropped. At 11px a row it turns to dither: you can see the year darken, but no week says anything and the texture competes with the lanes.

The blank rows are the one week off in August, drawn by nothing.

C — NOT CHOSEN. One ribbon, and the job is it.

The second ribbon here is SOBER, and look at what it draws: twenty-one identical cells, an unbroken column. That is a streak. No number counts it, but the eye does, and the day it breaks the screen will say so louder than any counter — the one thing this app promised not to do.

It also breaks the encoding: solid means enlarged and faded means diminished everywhere else, but here solid would mean yes and faded would mean no — a different question wearing the same clothes.

And it duplicates a lane that already exists. RECOVERY holds the meetings, the 12x12 and the step writing — the hours actually given. The ribbon even collides with that lane's colour.

One condition is a design. Two is a dashboard with a streak in it.

THE VALUE IS AT WRITE TIME, NOT READ TIME.

Every habit tracker puts its value at read time: log dutifully all year, get a chart. The logging is a tax you pay for the chart, which is why it degrades into bookkeeping inside a fortnight.

If Hollis is right that you know in the body within a second, then the tap is not data entry — it is a two-second somatic check on time you have already spent. That is the product. The year view is the receipt.

Three screens follow from taking that seriously. D puts your own sentence between you and the mechanics, so the pause lands on the reason rather than on the UI. E makes a changed why an event rather than an edit, because 'you find out when you read it and flinch' is only true if the flinch is recorded. F is the one that has to stay empty: the block joins the rail and nothing else happens, with the four things that did not happen listed underneath so that the silence reads as a decision.

DOOR 1 — TODAY, UNFINISHED. Axis: the day as the subject.

You open to a date and a question, with today's blocks as a short row of marks rather than a chart. The four lanes are the answer, so logging is not a button you find — it is the screen you are already on. The record moves one tap away at the bottom.

NOTHING, IT WAS THE JOB is a real answer, and the closest thing to a graceful exit for a day that had nothing in it.

Tradeoff: you are asked every single time you open the app, including the times you only came to look. A question you answer 'no' to daily becomes a nag without any of the machinery of a nag.

DOOR 2 — YOUR OWN WORDS. Axis: the lane speaks first.

One of your four why-sentences, nearly alone on the page, chosen by what the record already knows — here BODY, quiet since August. Not a nudge about the silence: just the sentence you wrote about why it matters, in your words, dated.

This is the purest form of 'remember the root cause daily'. It is also the only door of the three that says something you did not type into it that minute.

Tradeoff: rotation turns into wallpaper. By week six you will have read all four sentences forty times, and the surface that was supposed to re-body you is the surface you swipe past. Mitigations all look like variable rewards, which is the thing being refused.

DOOR 3 — THE BODY FIRST. Axis: the model's order, inverted.

Valence before lane. Hollis's claim is that the body answers within a second and the intellect arrives afterwards with reasons — so this asks the fast question first and the naming second. It is the only one of the three that changes the data model's order rather than just the furniture.

It is also the most honest about what the app is: a two-second somatic check, with bookkeeping attached.

Tradeoff: it presumes you have something to log, so the escape hatch has to be permanent furniture. And answering valence before naming the block risks rating the MOOD you walked in with rather than the hours — which is already the thing I am least confident about in the whole model.
